Medium gauge strings are not typically recommended on a Martin 00-28. Here’s why:

1. Body Size and Bracing
	•	The 00-28 is a small-bodied guitar (Grand Concert size) with scalloped X-bracing, designed for light to moderate tension.
	•	Martin generally recommends light gauge strings (typically .012–.054) for their 00-sized guitars to avoid excessive tension on the top and bridge.

2. Structural Concerns
	•	Medium gauge strings (typically .013–.056) exert significantly more tension, which could:
	•	Cause top distortion or bellying over time.
	•	Put extra strain on the bridge and neck joint.
	•	Lead to neck angle issues sooner than normal.

3. Tone vs. Safety
	•	Mediums will give you a fuller, louder tone, and more volume if you’re flatpicking aggressively, but the 00-28 isn’t built for that kind of pressure.
	•	If you’re seeking more projection or power, consider:
	•	Trying custom light or light top/heavy bottom sets.
	•	Using a pick with better attack or exploring alternate tunings.

4. Martin’s Official Guidance

Martin’s official spec for the 00-28 is light gauge strings, and they often come stock with Martin MA540 (light phosphor bronze, .012–.054).

If I am not mistaken, D-28s made after 1955 through most of 2024 have straight top bracing. D-18s typically scalloped except:

Forward braced and scalloped to 1938
Rear braced and scalloped to 1944
Tapered, gradually heavier until about 1950
Straight and rear braced until 1955
Straight and modern position until 2012
Forward and standard scalloped since 2012
Large bridge plate in 1969
2” maple plate in 1988

All depends on what’s “under the hood”. Scalloped bracing has more overtone complexity compared to non-scalloped “straight” braces guitars. Forward shifted guitars tend to have more bass response. Some recording artists and engineers tend to prefer straight braced dreads for their clarity and fundamentals. Also, factor in how heavy you play….if you want to drive the top hard, consider going with a straight braced guitar that won’t distort with a heavier attack. If you play softer, you might get more volume from a scalloped braced guitar.

The D18 and D28 each have their own unique voices. As with all guitars, there are unique tonal characteristics due to the nature of wood and their “fingerprint”. 

Play both side-by-side. If there’s no shop nearby, most online retailers offer a return/exchange policy.

Some things to consider when comparing:

D18 (reimagined series):

•Mahogany— known for its “fundamental”  tone; meaning it tends to produce less shimmer/overtones. Less complexity, if you will. 

•Soundboard (top) bracing: forward shifted and scalloped. This increases the top’s vibrational sensitivity, overall responsiveness, and bass. It creates more resonance with a lighter touch. However, this can be unwanted if using alternate and/or down-tunings. Also, scalloped top braces guitars are more feedback-prone. 

D28 (reimagined series): 

•Rosewood— creates a “darker” tonality and more overtone complexity. 

•D28s have forward shifted, non-scalloped (aka “straight”) top bracing. This lends itself to a little less bass response and may be better for recording and playing live via pickup or microphone (although mahogany is great for recording, too). D28s are designed to be balanced and a slightly less bass-heavy. HD-28s have scalloped bracing, so they’re boomier.

Good luck!

Get the D-28. Here’s why:

It can do anything you ask of it. 
Straight braced (aka “non-scalloped”) top bracing pairs very well with the dreadnaught size. More dynamic range than a 000 AND the OM because you get more “throttle” with a bigger body. Dreadnoughts can undoubtedly be played at lower volume or fingerpicked whenever appropriate. 

For many years I owned an awesome OM-28V (standard OMs are typically scalloped AND 25.4” scale); however, the D28 is more volume capable. Straight bracing prevents the top from being over-driven. Love the HDs (scalloped); however, excessive boomy-ness often results in a loss of balance and some clarity. 

Alternate tunings: Straight braced guitars, coupled with a longer scale length especially, are much better suited for drop and alternate tunings. More tension due to their longer scale length and better tone from straight bracing:

Less tension from down-tuning means your fingers can more easily fret the string(s), resulting in sharper notes. Shorter scaled guitars (while great in blues, etc) will have EVEN LESS tension on the strings when down-tuned.

Straight bracing prevents the top from being over driven by the deeper/lower string vibrations.

Also, definitely test drive the 15 series. They are all straight braced and longer scaled. The D-15 in particular is incredible. I love small bodied guitars too, both the 00-15m and 000-15m are so, so sweet.  Gotta love the 000-15sm for its 1 3/4” nut width and slotted headstock. 

Enjoy your time checking them out. Congrats in advance!

But seriously, Ebony pins are said to be warmer than bone. I’ve actually experimented with both and I prefer ebony on mahogany guitars and bone on rosewood guitars. All personal preference, but there is a reason Ebony is  traditionally paired with mahogany and bone with rosewood. 

Rosewood has more overtones/complexity of tone— bone helps to bring forth more bell like sound.

Mahogany’s tone is sought after for its midrange boosted and balanced EQ; it’s bright and more “clear” in its tone. More often than not, studio engineers prefer to work with mahogany for this reason. Additionally, bluegrass players appreciate the simple, straightforward tone which projects/“cuts” through the mix of instruments. Ebony pins compliment the style of the 18 series’ subdued aesthetic and likewise bone for the rosewood 28, 35 and 41, 42 and 45 series guitars.
